introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer ALL THE THREE QUESTIONS.

Question ONE carries THIRTY-FOUR marks and the rest carry THIRTY-THREE marks each.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Non Programmable Calculators Are Allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and Photograph.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) With map evidence only:

(i) Describe the relief and show how it constitutes a constraint to the horizontal expansion of Santa. (6 marks)

(ii) Describe the drainage characteristics of the entire map (4 marks)

(iii) Suggest ONE measure each for relief and drainage that can be adopted to expand the Santa built-up area. (3 marks)

(iv) Suggest TWO reasons for the presence of the Bafut Ngemba Forest in the north east. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
*Evidence is read from the reproduction of the map; altitudes are approximate (check on the sheet supplied on the day). Quote grid references (easting then northing) where possible.*

**(a)(i) Relief and its constraint on the horizontal expansion of Santa (6 marks).**

*Description (3 marks).*

- **Highland area with a large range of height.** The land lies between about 1,500 m in the south and south-east and more than 2,300 m in the north-east (spot height 2,319 m near the Bafut Ngemba Forest, about 20-21 E and 56-57 N) and about 2,507 m at **Mt Lefo** in the east (about 23-24 E, 51 N): a relative relief of roughly 1,000 m over 12 km.
- **Santa lies in a long, fairly low, gently sloping corridor** running north to south (contours of about 1,700 m on both sides of the town, about 17-19 E, 45-52 N), with widely spaced contours on the built-up area itself.
- **Steep slopes on both sides of the corridor.** To the east the contours are very close together on the flanks of the Mt Lefo massif (about 19-23 E, 48-52 N), forming a steep, deeply dissected slope with spurs and a steep escarpment; to the west and north-west there are hills of about 2,000 m (about 15-16 E, 49-51 N) and higher ground at the western edge of the map (2,000-2,100 m, about 11-12 E, 48-52 N) with closely spaced contours; the north-east is a high plateau-like block (2,100-2,300 m) under forest.
- **The relief is a rugged, dissected highland**: a succession of ridges, spurs and narrow valleys, with only small gently sloping areas (widely spaced contours) at the town, near Awing and in the south around Matazem.

*Constraint on horizontal (lateral) expansion (3 marks, any three developed points).*

- The built-up area is **elongated along the valley floor**, about 6 to 7 km long but only about 1 to 1.5 km wide: the steep slopes east and west of the corridor stop the town from spreading sideways.
- **Steep slopes (closely spaced contours) are costly and dangerous to build on**: cutting and levelling, retaining walls, difficult road access and a high risk of landslides, gullying and soil erosion in the rainy season.
- **Hills and ridges act as barriers** (the hills of about 2,000 m west of the town and the Mt Lefo massif east of it): they make the extension of roads, water and electricity networks expensive.
- **To the south the low, damp ground near Matazem, Mbu and Menka (swamp symbols) is poorly suited to building** (flooding, high water table), so expansion is also limited along the corridor.
- The little flat or gently sloping land available is also wanted for farming (arable land and market gardening on the map), so houses compete with farms.

*Marks: description 3; each developed constraint 1 (maximum 3).*

**(a)(ii) Drainage characteristics of the entire map (4 marks, any four points).**

- **Surface drainage is sparse**: only a few permanent streams are drawn on a large part of the map (north and centre), so the drainage density is low to moderate and many valleys appear dry or have only seasonal streams that the map does not show.
- **Streams are concentrated in the south and south-west**, around Menka and Matazem, where several small streams join and flow towards a low, swampy area (swamp symbol and a small waterbody about 14-16 E, 45-46.5 N); a stream also runs along the western edge of Santa from north to south towards Mbu.
- **Pattern:** streams follow the valleys and branch like the veins of a leaf (a **dendritic** pattern) where several join; they start on the high ground and flow down the slopes to the lowest land in the south and south-west (to be checked on the sheet).
- **Standing water:** the only large waterbody is **Lake Awing** in the north-east, lying in a hollow in the forested highlands and apparently without a stream flowing in or out on the map; a small waterbody is also shown north-west of Akum.
- **Poorly drained patches:** swamps in the southern low ground show impeded drainage where the valley floor is flat.

*Marks: 1 per accurate and illustrated point (four points).*

**(a)(iii) ONE measure each for relief and drainage (3 marks).**

- **Relief (1.5 marks):** build on the gentler spurs and on terraced, levelled platforms with retaining walls ("cut and fill"), lay out roads along the contours with gentle gradients, and build upwards (multi-storey houses) so that the town can grow without climbing steep slopes.
- **Drainage (1.5 marks):** drain and reclaim the swampy low ground in the south with drainage channels and culverts, and build storm drains and bridges along the streams, so that this land can be used safely for housing without flooding (keeping a strip along the river banks free).

**(a)(iv) TWO reasons for the Bafut Ngemba Forest in the north-east (3 marks, any two).**

- **Relief:** the forest lies on high and very steep slopes (2,000 to more than 2,300 m, closely spaced contours), too steep and too cold for farming and building, so the natural forest has not been cleared (1.5 marks).
- **Protection:** it is a protected forest reserve (the map shows a bold dashed boundary along its southern side): a watershed protecting the streams and Lake Awing and a habitat for biodiversity, so cutting and farming are controlled (1.5 marks).
- Other acceptable points: the cool, wet highland climate favours montane forest; the area is remote and has few roads, so it has little pressure from settlement.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) With the aid of sketch map show the site and situation of the town of Santa (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Definitions (1 mark).** The **site** is the actual ground on which the town is built; the **situation** is the position of the town in relation to its surroundings (neighbouring places, routes, relief and resources).

**Site (1.5 marks).** Santa stands on a long, narrow, gently sloping corridor (a valley-like depression) about 1,600-1,800 m high and running north to south; it is built along the **Trans-national road**, about 6-7 km long and 1-1.5 km wide. It is bordered by steep slopes to the east (Mt Lefo massif) and by hills of about 2,000 m to the west; a stream runs along its western side (a possible source of water) and low, swampy land lies to the south around Mbu and Matazem.

**Situation (1.5 marks).** Santa is a route centre on the Trans-national road, with Akum and the road to the north (towards Bamenda), and the road continuing south beyond the sheet; villages such as Alatening and Baba II lie to the north-west and west, Awing and the Bafut Ngemba Forest to the north-east, Mt Lefo to the east, and Mbu, Matazem and Menka to the south. It is surrounded by farmland (arable land, market gardening, orchards) which it serves as a market and service centre.

**Sketch map (marks included above).** Draw a frame with a title, north arrow and an approximate scale; show the built-up area as an elongated north-south shape, the Trans-national road through it, the hills east and west, the forest and Lake Awing in the north-east, the stream and the swampy ground, the neighbouring places and a key. A model is given below.

![fig-5](gce-al-geography-2025-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Marks: definitions 1; site described 1.5; situation described 1.5, with a neat labelled sketch carrying the credit (the sketch map may replace part of the text).*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Calculate the Detour Index of the section of the Trans-national road from Mile 12 (1751) to the northern extreme. (4 marks)

(ii) State the significance of the result obtained. (2 marks)

(iii) Suggest TWO actions that can be taken to reduce deviations along the Trans-national road. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(c)(i) Detour Index (4 marks).**

**Formula (1 mark).** The Detour Index compares the real length of a route with the straight line between its two ends:

$$
\text{Detour Index} = \frac{\text{actual route distance}}{\text{straight-line distance}} \quad (\times 100 \text{ if expressed as a percentage})
$$

**Measurements (2 marks).** The map scale is 1:50 000, so 2 cm on the map represent 1 km. Measure with a piece of thread laid along the road from Mile 12 (grid square 1751) to the northern edge of the map, then lay the thread on the scale bar. Measure the straight line with a ruler (or the grid, each square being 1 km).

- Actual road distance (following the bends, including the sharp turn at the junction about 16 E, 56 N): about **8.0 km** (about 16 cm on the 1:50 000 sheet).
- Straight-line distance (from Mile 12, about 17.3 E, 51.7 N, to the road at the northern edge, about 16.9 E, 57.9 N): about **6.3 km** (about 12.6 cm).

**Calculation (1 mark).**

$$
\text{Detour Index} = \frac{8.0\ \text{km}}{6.3\ \text{km}} \approx 1.27 \quad (\approx 127\%)
$$

*These values come from the reduced reproduction and are approximate; the examiner accepts a value between 1.2 and 1.35 (120 to 135 per cent) if the method, the two distances and the units are shown.*

**(c)(ii) Significance (2 marks).** A value of 1.27 means that the road is about 27 per cent longer than the direct line: it is **moderately winding (indirect)**, far from the ideal value of 1 (100 per cent) for a perfectly straight road. The road bends round the spurs, hills and valleys of this rugged highland, which raises the distance, travel time, fuel cost and risk of accidents for traffic and goods between Mile 12 and Akum; it also shows that relief strongly controls the layout of the transport network.

**(c)(iii) TWO actions to reduce deviations (2 marks, 1 each).**

- **Straighten the road (realignment):** cut through the spurs and fill hollows (cut and fill), or build bridges over the valleys, so that sharp bends and hairpins (for example at the junction) are removed.
- **Build a bypass or shortcut and improve the road:** a new direct link between the main points, plus widening, a good tarred surface and signs, so that the effective journey time falls even where the distance cannot be shortened (tunnels are another costly option).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Identify and justify the environmental problem portrayed by the photograph. (2 marks)

(ii) Suggest two possible causes of the problem identified (2 marks)

(iii) State two measures that can be adopted to overcome the identified problem (2 marks)

![fig-4](gce-al-geography-2025-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*SEPARATE SHEET (INSERT) IN COLOUR. Photo for Question 1d(i). Figure 1: Photo of settlement.*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(d)(i) The problem and its justification (2 marks).** The photograph shows an **urban slum (informal or squatter settlement, shanty town)** with its environmental and health problems: overcrowding and unplanned housing, poor sanitation and pollution.

*Justification (any two observations, 1 mark each, 2 marks with the identification):* houses are very close to each other and built of makeshift materials (corrugated iron sheets, planks, old tyres on some roofs); there is no regular street plan, only narrow irregular paths; no drains or organised open spaces are visible between the shelters; and the planned houses with ordered roofs on the far hill and the open land in between contrast with the congested foreground.

**(d)(ii) TWO possible causes (2 marks, 1 each).**

- **Rural-urban migration and rapid urban growth:** people arrive in the city faster than formal housing and jobs are created.
- **Poverty, unemployment and a shortage of affordable housing and serviced land:** the poor cannot buy or rent formal houses and build cheaply where they can.
- Also acceptable: weak town planning and poor control of land use, high land prices, land tenure problems, natural population growth.

**(d)(iii) TWO measures (2 marks, 1 each).**

- **Upgrade the slum or resettle its people:** provide water, drainage, toilets, rubbish collection, roads and electricity, or move households to planned housing estates (site and service schemes).
- **Plan and build affordable housing and control land use:** enforce town planning rules, make serviced land available and create jobs, together with rural development to slow the flow of migrants to the city (rural development, decentralisation).

*Marks: identification and justification 2; causes 2; measures 2.*
